case.label: E
case.text: Elastic Beanstalk is a managed platform that handles provisioning, patching of the platform and scaling, so a small team could call it low overhead for a daily job and say it meets the no-inbound-access need. It still runs EC2 instances that the environment manages, is not serverless, and the stem asks for no instance patching or scaling, so it loses to Fargate options. A careful candidate could also argue Lambda (D) is intended as a serverless pick, but the 2 to 3 hour run exceeds the 15 minute Lambda limit, so it is excluded.

answers.flag: Neither the key nor option A says the nightly stop must change to a hibernate call, so the stem leaves open whether replacing instances alone meets the memory requirement, and A is a defensible (if higher-effort) second path.

case.label: A
case.text: Option A also launches replacements with hibernation and an encrypted root volume, which is the only way to get hibernation (it cannot be turned on for running instances). Ten instances is a small number, and hand launching avoids building a template, so a candidate could say it meets the requirements. It only loses on the LEAST operational overhead tiebreaker, and it does not mention sizing the root volume for 32 GiB of memory.

case.label: A
case.text: A 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the largest discount and the stem says the family stays in the Region for 3 years, so a candidate could pick it as most cost-effective. But a Savings Plan is only a billing discount and reserves no capacity, so it cannot meet the always-available capacity requirement. Option D has the same defect; option B meets capacity but at the full On-Demand rate.
